brief: A herb planter of three cells side by side, each with a bin that drains.

requirements.evidence: Three full bases (piece:0,0,0, piece:1,0,0, piece:2,0,0) in one straight row, bolted together with two joint bolts.

requirements.requirement: Each cell has a bin that drains
requirements.evidence: Each cell holds a full-depth drained bin (hex-bin-full-drain). How well it drains in real use hasn't been tested; the configurator only checks fit.
All three bins are filled with soil and planted with young basil, parsley and mint (prop:4, prop:5, prop:6). These plants are staging only, not parts.

finish.summary: I built a three-cell herb planter. Three full bases sit side by side in one row, at q=0, 1 and 2 with r=0. Each cell holds one full-depth drained bin (hex-bin-full-drain). Following the house rules, I closed the 14 open faces with solid end caps and bolted the two joints between cells, which makes 20 parts. Each bin is filled with soil to the rim and planted with one young herb: basil, parsley and mint. The final check found no rule issues and no prop warnings, and the mesh check was clear. All three plants show in the view from above.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
